title: When the measure becomes the work
author: Myatt, Mary
summary: Mary Myatt applies Jerry Muller's concept of 'metric fixation'—the belief that professional work can be reduced to numerical indicators providing objective evidence of quality—to schools. The central problem is not that schools measure learning but that internally generated KS3 data gradually acquires authority it doesn't deserve, and the goal shifts from developing understanding to moving numbers. When teachers exhaust themselves serving the measurement system, the system has been served but the learning hasn't.
points: Metric fixation enters schools through reasonable motives—tracking progress, identifying need, assuring parents—but becomes pathological when the measure stops serving the work and starts becoming the work.
Internal KS3 data lacks the reliability of national assessments; a change in a number might reflect better understanding, a harder task, a different marker, or simply ordinary performance variation.
Numbers appear neutral but conceal prior decisions about what to measure, how to measure it, and what to leave out—the things easiest to count gradually displace what matters most.
A pupil who ticked every guitar outcome box never learned to play; the one who aimed to perform for an audience eventually composed original music—the messier journey produced the real learning.

Useful assessment discussion focuses on what pupils understood, where misconceptions remain, and whether the curriculum is producing the intended intellectual work—not on moving numbers up a spreadsheet.
When teachers spend weekends writing careful comments that pupils glance at before moving on, the system has been served but the learning hasn't—this is metric fixation made visible.
quotes: In The Tyranny of Metrics, Jerry Muller describes “metric fixation”: the belief that complex professional work can be reduced to numerical indicators, that those indicators provide objective evidence of quality, and that attaching consequences to them will improve performance.
Internally generated KS3 data does not have the reliability of national assessments taken by large numbers of pupils, marked against common criteria and moderated at scale.
We want to know how pupils are doing, we want to identify where support is needed, and we want to assure parents, governors and leaders that pupils are making progress.
The journey was less tidy and less easily captured, but over time the pupil learned chords, developed confidence and eventually performed an original composition.
It means discussing what pupils have understood, where misconceptions remain and whether the curriculum is producing the intellectual work we intended.
In assessment, this can mean collecting information because the system requires it, rather than because it will change what happens next.
The comments are barely read, there’s is little time to improve the work, and the teacher is exhausted, but the system has been served.
